newsitem.title: USA: U.S. banks stake claim to issuing electronic money.
newsitem.headline: U.S. banks stake claim to issuing electronic money.

text.p: While paper money is unlikely to be displaced for a long time, electronic money is the growth area of the future and banks should be the only institutions allowed to issue it, a U.S. banking trade group said on Sunday.
In a report on the payments system of the future, the American Bankers Association (ABA) recommended that "issuance of third-party instruments should be limited to regulated depository institutions."
The report was released at the group's convention here and it was the first time the ABA had staked out a position on the issue, which will be the subject of continued discussion.

"Failure of an issuer of third-party payments instruments has the potential to disrupt the payments system, for it could derail final settlement of thousands of transactions and leave thousands of consumers with devalued or worthless payments instruments," the report warned.
Such an occurrence could shake public confidence and would likely result in heavy regulation, the report said.

Even with a high growth rate in electronic money, it would take a long time for it to displace paper money, but it is an area the banking industry must look at, James Chessen, ABA's chief economist, said.

One driver of change would be demographics, he said. The so-called Generation X, aged 18 to 34, represents about one-third of U.S. bank customers and they were fairly comfortable using computers and technology, he said.
The concern is not with two-party transactions, such as stored-value cards used for travel on underground trains in cities such as Washington, James Culberson, past president of ABA, said.

But rather the concern would be if more parties were involved, such as one firm issuing a "smart" card that could be used to buy items at other businesses, he said. Smart cards look similar to credit cards with a chip embedded for a certain amount of money.
American bankers are also concerned about competition from other businesses that are not as regulated as their industry.

"You have to remember that we have so many regulations in our business, and if we allow somebody else into the same business we're in without those same regulations, we can be cut out totally," Culberson said.
The report will be circulated to bankers. Former Federal Reserve Governor John LaWare was a consultant to the task force that produced it, the ABA said.
